title: Ravioli all'uovo
subtitle: Single-yolk fresh ravioli, nido d'uovo
excerpt: Individual fresh pasta squares, each enclosing a whole egg yolk in a ricotta nest, sealed and poached until the yolk is just set. Served with brown butter and Parmesan. A showpiece dish from the Italian alta cucina tradition.
sourceNotes: Raviolo all'uovo (singular: raviolo), also known as the 'nido d'uovo' or egg nest raviolo, is a dish associated with the Bolognese restaurant San Domenico and its chef Nino Bergese, who popularised it in the 1980s. The technique of enclosing an intact egg yolk in a pasta cushion is widely documented in Italian alta cucina cookbooks. This version synthesises the method as it appears across multiple Italian restaurant-cooking references.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cannot be frozen: the egg yolk would solidify and the pasta would become waterlogged.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The assembled ravioli can be refrigerated on a floured tray for up to 2 hours before cooking. Any longer and the pasta begins to absorb moisture from the ricotta.

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian for 'to the tooth': pasta cooked until it is just firm when bitten, with no raw flour taste but not yet soft.

content.text: Each raviolo all'uovo is a single large parcel. It has an outer skin of fresh egg pasta, a nest of ricotta seasoned with herbs and Parmesan, and in the centre, an intact whole egg yolk. When the raviolo is poached and cut open at the table, the yolk runs into the butter sauce. It is a striking dish and a technically demanding one. The pasta must be thin. The ricotta nest must hold the yolk securely. The timing in the boiling water must be precise enough to leave the yolk liquid.

items.prepNote: plus 4 extra yolks for the filling
drained in a sieve for 30 minutes
yolks only, kept whole and intact; carefully separated

content.text: Make the pasta: mound the flour on a work surface, make a well in the centre, and crack in the 2 whole eggs. Beat the eggs with a fork, gradually incorporating the flour, then knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap in cling film and rest for 30 minutes.

Make the filling: stir the drained ricotta, grated Parmesan, and chives together in a bowl. Season with salt. The mixture should be firm enough to pipe or spoon into a ring without collapsing. Transfer to a piping bag fitted with a plain nozzle, or keep in a bowl.
Roll the pasta as thinly as possible, to about 1 to 2 mm. Cut into 8 squares of approximately 12 cm each (two squares per raviolo).

On each of 4 squares, pipe or spoon a ring of ricotta filling in the centre, leaving a 4 cm gap in the middle. Very carefully lower one whole egg yolk into the gap in the ricotta ring. The yolk must stay intact.

Brush the edges of the pasta square with a little water. Lay a second pasta square on top, pressing gently around the filling to expel any air pockets, then seal the edges firmly. Trim to neaten. Place on a lightly floured tray and refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Melt the butter in a wide frying pan with the sage leaves over medium heat until the butter turns a light golden brown and smells nutty. Remove from the heat.

Bring a very large, wide pan of heavily salted water to a gentle, not violent, boil. Lower the ravioli in one at a time. Cook for exactly 3 minutes. The yolk should be warm and barely set; the pasta should be
. Lift out carefully with a wide slotted spoon or spider.
Place each raviolo on a warm plate. Spoon the brown butter and sage over the top. Finish with freshly grated Parmesan and serve immediately, telling each guest to cut into the raviolo at the table.

items.cause: Cooked for too long, or water at a rolling boil rather than a gentle simmer
items.fix: 3 minutes at a gentle boil is the target. A violent boil will cook the yolk through. Taste the pasta of one raviolo first if you are uncertain.

items.symptom: Pasta seals tear and filling leaks
items.cause: Air trapped inside, or seal not pressed firmly enough
items.fix: Expel all air when pressing the top sheet down. Seal edges well by pressing with fingertips, not a fork which can pierce the pasta.

items.symptom: Ricotta nest collapses when the yolk is placed in it
items.fix: Drain the ricotta for at least 30 minutes in a fine sieve before using. It must hold its shape when piped.

content.text: Raviolo all'uovo is a dish of the Italian alta cucina, born in the grand restaurant kitchens of Emilia-Romagna. It is now a staple of Italian fine dining worldwide. It appears on the menus of Michelin-starred restaurants from London to New York. Cutting it open at the table and watching the yolk run is one of the most satisfying moments in a restaurant meal. At home it requires patience and precision but no special equipment beyond a rolling pin, a piping bag, and a wide, gentle pan of water.
